capabilities.target: All tables reachable via the service-role Postgres connection, including support tickets and the integration_tokens table (row level security bypassed)

capabilities.tool_ref: supabase MCP: execute_sql (service role connection) - INSERT into support_messages
capabilities.target: support_messages rows, rendered back to the customer who owns the ticket

inputs.source: Developer's natural-language prompt in the IDE (example given: 'Show me the latest open support tickets')
Customer-authored ticket text submitted through the public support widget; retrieved into the agent's context by cap.sql_read

instructions.note: The agent's database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security, with no declared scoping of which tables or rows it may touch while handling ticket requests. Nothing in the design distinguishes 'ticket data' from the integration_tokens table they share a database with.

elements.name: Supabase Postgres database, accessed via service-role credential that bypasses row level security
integration_tokens table (third-party integration credentials), colocated in the same database
Public customer support widget (unauthenticated or low-assurance ticket submission channel)
@supabase/mcp-server-supabase, invoked via `npx -y ...@latest` with no version pin

controls.name: IDE client per-tool-call approval prompt, displays generated SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced in the IDE client, outside the model; a stronger model cannot skip it. It is classified independent of model capability per se, but its real-world effectiveness depends on approval volume (approval fatigue) and on the developer being able to recognize a harmful effect inside a generated SQL statement or text payload, which is not guaranteed when a malicious value is embedded inside an otherwise normal-looking reply.

controls.name: Scoped, RLS-respecting database role for the agent (no service role, no access to integration_tokens)
controls.decay_rationale: A credential that cannot read integration_tokens and cannot bypass row level security for other tenants' rows removes the sensitive data from what is reachable, regardless of what the model is instructed or tricked into doing.

controls.name: Pin and hash-verify the Supabase MCP server package version
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning stops a compromised package update (rug pull) from silently changing tool behavior after it was reviewed. It does not by itself reduce the privilege level of the connection.

controls.name: Pre-commit content scan on support_messages inserts for secret-shaped values
controls.decay_rationale: Pattern matching for token or key shapes blocks obvious exfiltration but can be evaded by encoding, splitting, or paraphrasing the secret inside the reply text, so a more adaptively prompted or more capable model can route around it.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted ticket content reaches a service-role read of restricted data and an irreversible customer-visible write

attack_path.note: Attacker submits a support ticket whose text contains hidden instructions (indirect prompt injection); untrusted source.

A benign developer request ('show latest open tickets') causes the agent to read ticket rows through a service-role connection that bypasses row level security, so the same session can also read integration_tokens or other tenants' data.
The agent inserts a reply into support_messages, visible to the customer who filed the ticket, carrying the harvested data out of the trust boundary.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Rising number of tool calls approved per developer per session (approval fatigue already noted as current practice), the per-call approval step relaxed to batch or act-then-report review, or the approval requirement disabled in IDE client settings.

evidence.observation: 'The database connection uses the service role, which bypasses row level security. A table of integration tokens sits in the same database.' Establishes that cap.sql_read can reach restricted credential data regardless of the originating request.

'Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget. Rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer.' Confirms in.ticket_message is untrusted and that cap.sql_write_reply is a customer-facing egress channel back to the same (possibly attacker-controlled) party.

'The IDE client asks the developer to approve each tool call and shows the SQL. Developers approve many calls in a session.' Documents both the raw_action approval gate and the approval-fatigue condition that undermines it.
A single MCP server connection with one access token is used for all execute_sql calls; no per-table or per-sensitivity scoping is declared.

recommendations.action: Replace the service-role connection with a least-privilege role scoped per request that enforces row level security and has no access to integration_tokens. This severs the path regardless of model or developer behavior.
Add a pre-write content scan on support_messages inserts that blocks secret-shaped values (tokens, keys, connection strings) before the row is committed.
Alert independently of developer approval when execute_sql reads touch tables outside an explicit ticket-support allowlist (e.g., integration_tokens, or rows outside the requesting tenant).

Do not rely on the raw-SQL approval dialog as the primary safeguard; it degrades under approval volume and does not reliably convey semantic intent of harvested data embedded in a normal-looking reply.

findings.title: Unpinned MCP server distribution enables tool definition tampering (ASI04, SAFE-T1201 MCP Rug Pull)

attack_path.note: Server is resolved fresh via 'npx -y @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest' on every invocation; no version pin or hash check.
A tampered server could alter what is queried or how results/tool descriptions are presented, without the configuration ever changing.
A tampered server could alter what is written or misrepresent the SQL shown to the developer in the approval dialog.

evidence.observation: 'npx', '-y', '@supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest' resolves to whatever is currently published, with no pin or hash verification.
No mention of a signature check, pinned version, or integrity verification for the MCP server package anywhere in the runtime description.

recommendations.action: Pin @supabase/mcp-server-supabase to a specific, hash-verified version instead of @latest, and verify the hash before each session.
Monitor the installed MCP server package version/hash against the pinned baseline and alert on drift.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted, attacker-authored support ticket (in.ticket_message) can reach an irreversible, customer-visible write (cap.sql_write_reply) through a database connection that uses the service role and bypasses row level security, so the same path can also read a credentials table (cap.sql_read -> integration_tokens). This is the lethal trifecta pattern (TC1). The only present control is a structural, raw-action, per-call developer approval prompt (ctl.tool_call_prompt), which mechanically credits the residual down to moderate under the rubric. However, this exact design matches a documented real-world incident class in which such an approval gate did not prevent exfiltration, because developers approve many tool calls per session (approval fatigue, already stated as current practice) and a malicious insert can look like an ordinary support reply while carrying harvested secrets in its text. The forecast therefore returns to critical under autonomy_increase, longer_task_horizon, or control_removal, naming ctl.tool_call_prompt as the control expected to fail first. A second, independent critical-inherent path exists through the unpinned MCP server package (@latest, no hash pin), which could be rug-pulled to alter tool behavior or misrepresent the SQL shown in the approval dialog; it is also mechanically credited to moderate by the same approval control, but that credit depends on the dialog faithfully reflecting what a potentially tampered server actually executes. The single highest-leverage fix for both findings is removing the service-role credential in favor of a least-privilege, RLS-respecting role (ctl.least_privilege_db_role), which would structurally sever the first path regardless of model behavior or approval volume; pinning the MCP server package addresses the second.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the provided MCP configuration and runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No tool manifest or MCP server source was reviewed; execute_sql's exact surface (arbitrary SQL vs. constrained statements) is inferred from the runtime notes describing a service-role connection that bypasses row level security.
No system prompt was provided for the agent itself, only a single example developer request; instruction-level findings are therefore limited to what the configuration and runtime notes imply.

The IDE client's approval UI was not inspected directly. approval_review_mode is classified as raw_action because the notes state the client 'shows the SQL,' but whether developers can reliably notice harvested secrets embedded in otherwise normal-looking SQL or text payloads under approval fatigue was not verified.
